name: Cistanche

lead: Cistanche is the dried stem of a parasitic desert plant used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and vitality tonic. In bodybuilding forums it is mentioned as a testosterone or DHT booster and as part of post-cycle herb stacks, taken for libido, strength and recovery.

The chain is a claimed testosterone and DHT rise leading to better strength and recovery. Research so far is mostly lab and animal work on compounds such as echinacoside and acteoside, plus a few small human trials on strength, cognition and fatigue; none found measured testosterone or DHT.

paras: Extracts are taken as capsules or powders, often stacked with other herbs, including after steroid cycles. Users take it daily for weeks and judge libido, energy and training.
Trials reported so far are small and short, and it is approved as a food ingredient in China. Long-term safety data in healthy men are limited, and wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II.

forums.title: Do These Herbs Cause Organ Damage?

angle.text: Cistanche is a Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums describe as a testosterone and DHT booster, taken for libido, strength and recovery, including after cycles. Small human trials have looked at strength, cognition and fatigue rather than hormone levels.

lead: Cistanche is a genus of parasitic desert plants whose fleshy stems, chiefly from Cistanche deserticola and Cistanche tubulosa, are used as a tonic in traditional Chinese medicine under the name Rou Cong Rong, sometimes called "desert ginseng" [1][2][3]. Traditional uses include treating kidney deficiency, impotence, female infertility and constipation in older people [3].

In bodybuilding and testosterone-optimisation communities, Cistanche tubulosa extract is sold as a herbal supplement and is described by some users as a test booster or a DHT booster, often stacked with other herbs during post-cycle therapy [4][5][6]. Laboratory and animal research has examined its phenylethanoid glycosides (echinacoside, acteoside) for antioxidant, neuroprotective, liver-protective and bone-related effects [1][7].

Human trials of Cistanche extracts are few and small. They have looked at muscle strength and recovery, locomotive function, cognition and fatigue [8][9][10]. No published trial identified here has measured testosterone-raising or DHT-raising effects as a cosmetic or physique outcome.
infobox: Wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II; approved as a food ingredient in China from 2016

paras: The genus Cistanche belongs to the family Orobanchaceae. Its members lack chlorophyll and draw nutrients from the roots of host shrubs in arid regions [11]. The dried stems are the medicinal part [1].

Reviews describe the main active-compound classes as phenylethanoid glycosides, iridoids, lignans and polysaccharides [3]. Wild populations were once endangered, and large-scale cultivation has since turned the herb into a major commercial product in China, with an estimated annual output of about 6,000 tons.

In traditional Chinese medicine the herb is classed as a kidney-yang tonic. It is used for impotence, infertility, weakness of the lower back and knees, and constipation [3][2]. Modern review articles list proposed pharmacological actions such as anti-ageing, antioxidant, neuroprotective, hepatoprotective, immunomodulatory and bone-promoting effects, mostly from cell and animal work [1][2].

On the T Nation forum, users list Cistanche tubulosa among herbs added to post-cycle recovery or testosterone-support regimens alongside tongkat ali, ashwagandha, DIM and others [4][5]. One user lists it as a "DHT boost" in a supplement routine [6]. Another thread asks whether a list of herbs that includes Cistanche carries a risk of organ damage [12].

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2025 enrolled 48 men, half resistance-trained and half untrained, to test Cistanche deserticola supplementation on muscle strength and recovery [8]. A related registration describes a study of Cistanche on anaerobic performance and recovery in men with different training levels [13].

Other randomized trials have tested Cistanche tubulosa extract on locomotive syndrome in older adults [9], a Cistanche tubulosa and Ginkgo biloba combination on cognitive function in middle-aged and older people [14], and a Ginkgo and Cistanche product on fatigue symptoms [10]. A trial in men with central obesity combined an extract with aerobic exercise [15]. A Chinese granule formula was tested for tinnitus in chronic nephritis [16].

A 2025 systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia is listed among related literature, but the summary available does not report Cistanche-specific findings [17]. No trial found here has tested Cistanche for testosterone or DHT levels as a primary outcome.

Traditional use and Chinese food-ingredient approval are cited in reviews as indications of acceptable tolerability, but the human trials above are small and short. A forum thread raises the question of organ damage from herbal supplements including Cistanche, without presenting data [12]. A topical herbal patch containing Cistanche deserticola is listed in the US DailyMed database as an unapproved product marketed for prostate-related symptoms [18].
